newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians hope for money back from pyramid schemes.
newsitem.headline: Albanians hope for money back from pyramid schemes.

text.p: Albanians lining up outside offices of failed "pyramid" investment schemes said on Wednesday they hoped against hope that they would get some of their money back.

The collapse of the get-rich-quick schemes in which many Albanians had invested their life savings triggered an armed insurrection in late February. At least 300 people have been killed in the violence.

"I have to hope. I prefer to die than to lose my life savings. They are for my two children," Flutra Laci, a middle-aged housewife, told Reuters outside the offices of one scheme, which is still promising to repay investors.
Laci said she had sold her home and invested $12,000 in the scheme last October after seeing her friends earn generous interest payouts of eight percent per month.
Three months after she deposited her money, the interest payments stopped. "I am trying to get my capital back. I don't care about the interest," Laci said.
Earlier this month, Finance Minister Arben Malaj said pyramid savings schemes were worth about half the national income of Europe's poorest country.

Gross domestic product in the country of 3.4 million people was $2.3 billion in 1996, and the pyramid schemes had probably attracted $1-1.2 billion, he said. Parliament banned pyramid schemes in January.

Outside the offices of one scheme, teacher Mersin Hoxhalli, 32, said he had sold his modest house in the south and invested the money in several pyramid schemes, hoping to buy a better house in the capital Tirana. This scheme had paid him no interest for three months.
"Now I just want my capital back," Hoxhalli said. "I'm optimistic. After all, I didn't invest a big sum. I hope to get it back."

In a daily ritual, dozens of Albanians lined up outside the offices of one company and peered at a list posted on a notice-board which announced account numbers due to pay out that day. Thinly staffed offices handed out small payments.
Local residents say some of the account numbers are fictitious and the long lists give the impression that the companies are in better financial shape than they really are.

No one stood outside the office of another well-known scheme, Silva, based in a green mansion in central Tirana, because it had posted a notice saying that it would not pay out funds until next Friday.
The notice said that Silva had faced administrative problems reimbursing people because of the closure of banks during the recent violence in the southern rebel-held city of Vlore, where it is based.
Much of the south is controlled by rebel committees, which blame President Sali Berisha, a northerner, for the failure of the savings plans.

Albanians questioned by Reuters said they had invested in the schemes after seeing intensive publicity on television and because they had seen their friends earn big interest payouts when the schemes began.
"I'm not angry that others made money. They were the lucky ones," said Hoxhalli.
Some people said they had trusted the pyramid companies as they appeared to be financially sound, but they had not known how their money was invested.

Ferit Ismaili, a pensioner who sank his entire family's life savings of $2,000 into one pyramid plan, said he had no idea how the company had invested his money. But he guessed it had been spent on building supermarkets and offices.
"I do hope to get some of my money back," he said. "But I also regret my decision to invest. It was me who took the decision, no-one forced me."
